source.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
source.authors: Jared Kaplan; Sam McCandlish; Tom Henighan; Tom B. Brown; Benjamin Chess; Rewon Child; Scott Gray; Alec Radford; Jeffrey Wu; Dario Amodei

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper directly measures language-model cross-entropy across model, dataset, training-time and compute scales, and tests architecture-shape effects. It is itself an original source for the central scaling claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports fitted scaling laws, allocation trends, and architecture comparisons as its own results. Results about downstream language-task capabilities are not reported; cited findings from other papers are not recorded as rows. Several plots are described in the text but provide no exact values, so those rows are marked figure_only.
record.test_reason: This is Kaplan et al., one of the original sources. Its own sweeps measure WebText2 test cross-entropy against non-embedding parameters, dataset tokens, steps and compute. It also fits compute-optimal allocation, varies Transformer shape at fixed N and evaluates loss on other text distributions. No verdict labels are given because the study is an original source for the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that loss scales as power laws in N, D and Cmin, depends weakly on shape, and that compute-optimal training favours large models stopped early. They also say the laws lack theory and must break down, at the latest near the projected intersection point.
record.recipe_differences: This paper is the original empirical study: autoregressive language-model training sweeps measuring cross-entropy against parameter count, dataset size, training steps and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported exponents differ slightly between separate and joint fits, and between fixed-batch and critical-batch-adjusted compute. The smallest dataset regime fits poorly; the paper also notes exclusions of some very small, one-layer and not-fully-converged runs in selected fits.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss on other text distributions tracks in-distribution loss with a roughly constant offset. It does not depend on training phase or depth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Out-of-distribution text loss is a function of in-distribution loss, independent of training duration.

fits_no_version.finding: Critical batch size follows a power law in loss (B* about 2e8 tokens, alpha_B about 0.21), independent of model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Critical batch size scales as a power of loss only.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-token loss scales as a power law in position within the context (Figure 20).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss falls as a power law in context position.

record.problems: The paper says it lacks a solid theoretical understanding and cannot systematically characterize corrections to the laws. The smallest-data fits are poor; regularization was not optimized across data and model sizes; compute estimates omit context-dependent terms; and the authors identify possible untuned hyperparameters. Several results are shown in figures without exact values in the text.

untested.parts: No prospective test: no fit on small runs was used to predict separately trained runs orders of magnitude larger.
Image, audio and video models, repeated-data regimes, and fine-tuning are not tested. Only zero-shot loss on other text distributions is measured.
Entirely untested; no downstream task performance is reported.
No comparison with other published laws, such as Hoffmann et al. Data and tokenization are not varied, and fitting method is not varied systematically.
Allocation exponents are measured only for WebText2 with the paper's fixed schedule. Stability across datasets and schedules is untested.

missing.what: Including embedding parameters in N obscures the trend and makes loss appear to depend strongly on depth. Excluding them gives a single trend. This is a parameter-counting choice that changes the law.
Learning-rate schedule is mostly irrelevant to converged loss if summed LR is large enough; run-to-run variation is about 0.05.
LSTMs and Universal Transformers also show loss-versus-N trends. LSTMs plateau on later tokens, and recurrent Transformers do slightly better per parameter.
The L(Cmin) exponent predicted from the L(N,Smin) fit is 0.054, versus 0.050 measured. This is a consistency check of the fitted laws.
The fixed-batch allocation N ∝ C^0.88 differs from the batch-adjusted N ∝ Cmin^0.73. The allocation exponent depends on the batch adjustment.

record.verdict_notes: This is an original source, so no labels are given. In Section 1.2, Kaplan's allocation (N ∝ C^0.73, D ∝ C^0.27) is stated as the empirical result. R9's D exponent is derived from B and S trends, not measured directly. Equation 6.7 gives D ∝ Cmin^0.26 with 4e10 tokens, slightly different from Table 6 (0.27, 2e10).

versions.untested_parts: None of the stated core factors is wholly untested; results concern autoregressive language models and the paper's stated training and dataset settings.

The paper reports extrapolation from early training curves and fitted relationships, but does not report a prospective test in which a fit to small runs is used to predict a separately held-out run orders of magnitude larger.
The allocation trend is tested for the paper's compute-efficient setup; it does not establish that the allocation exponents hold across other datasets, architectures or training regimes.
Tests vary selected Transformer shape parameters, not every architecture detail or a broad range of model families.
Tests transfer to other text distributions only. Other modalities, repeated-data regimes and fine-tuning are not tested.
Downstream task performance is not evaluated.
The paper compares selected fitting choices and discusses an eventual breakdown, but does not systematically vary all setup choices or compare the later published laws named in the claim.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (model-size scaling runs; aggregate)
rows.size_stated: 768 to 1.5 billion non-embedding parameters across the study
rows.stage_stated: autoregressive pretraining; models near convergence on WebText2
rows.operation_detail: Measured WebText2 test cross-entropy as non-embedding parameter count varied, with sufficiently large data.
rows.measure: Test cross-entropy loss L(N); fitted power law L(N) ≈ (Nc/N)^αN
rows.value: αN ∼ 0.076; Nc ∼ 8.8 × 10^13 non-embedding parameters (summary fit)
rows.note: The paper says the trend spans more than six orders of magnitude and reports no signs of deviation at the upper end of the observed range.
rows.check: Linked to V2, but this is an in-range fit of L(N), not a prediction of much larger held-out runs. Drop V2.

rows.subject: Transformer language model (dataset-size sweep; (nlayer, nembd) = (36, 1280))
rows.stage_stated: autoregressive pretraining; stopped when test loss ceased to decrease
rows.operation_detail: Measured test cross-entropy after training on fixed subsets of WebText2 of varying token count.
rows.measure: Test cross-entropy loss L(D); fitted power law L(D) ≈ (Dc/D)^αD
rows.value: αD ∼ 0.095; Dc ∼ 5.4 × 10^13 tokens (summary fit)
rows.note: The summary says trends span more than six orders of magnitude overall; the dataset-size sweep itself is reported over two orders of magnitude in the paper's summary of the scaling-law coverage.
rows.check: Linked to V2, but this is an in-range fit of L(D). Drop V2. The D sweep covers only about two orders of magnitude (22M to 23B tokens), per Section 1.2.

source_check.locator_found: Section 1.2, Equation (1.2); Section 3 opening sweep ranges; Section 3.3, Equation (3.2); Table 5.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (fixed-batch compute sweep; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared test loss of the best-performing model at each fixed-batch training-compute budget.
rows.measure: Test cross-entropy loss L(C); fitted power law
rows.value: αC = 0.057; Cc = 1.6 × 10^7 PF-days (Table 5)
rows.note: The paper cautions that fixed-batch results are not truly compute-optimal.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (compute-efficient frontier; aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: autoregressive pretraining; compute adjusted for critical batch size
rows.operation_detail: Measured and fitted loss against minimum compute Cmin, adjusting for batch-size efficiency.
rows.measure: Test cross-entropy loss L(Cmin); fitted power law
rows.value: αCmin ∼ 0.050; Ccmin ∼ 3.1 × 10^8 PF-days
rows.note: The paper identifies this adjusted trend, rather than the fixed-batch trend, as the one to use for predictions.

source_check.correct: V1: observed. V3: cannot_determine from this row; L(Cmin) measures optimal loss versus compute, not the parameter/token allocation powers. Remove V3 from this row; R7 and R9 measure that allocation.
source_check.problem: The observed loss power law establishes V1, but this measure alone cannot establish the V3 allocation claim.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (joint parameter and dataset-size sweep; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a joint loss function to models trained with varying parameter count and dataset size.
rows.measure: Test cross-entropy L(N,D), including the fitted scaling exponents
rows.note: The authors say these parameters differ slightly from the separate fits in Section 3 because this fits the full L(N,D) relationship.
rows.check: The V7 aspect (joint versus separate fit exponents) is already captured by R19. Keep this row on V1 only.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (training curves; aggregate)
rows.size_stated: multiple sizes; exact set not stated
rows.operation_detail: Fit training loss over parameter count and training steps after an initial transient period.
rows.measure: Test cross-entropy L(N,Smin) and training-curve fit
rows.note: The authors state that extrapolating the early part of a training curve can roughly predict the loss after much longer training; fits are imperfect and break down early in training.
rows.check: The extrapolation is from the early part of a training curve to longer training of the same model, not from small runs to much larger ones. The authors call the fits imperfect and say they break down early in training.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (empirical compute-efficient frontier; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the parameter count of the best-performing model at different compute budgets.
rows.measure: Optimal non-embedding parameter count N(Cmin)
rows.value: N(Cmin) ∝ (Cmin)^0.73; fitted form N = (1.3 × 10^9) Cmin^0.73
rows.note: The paper reports that optimal model size grows by 5x for each 10x increase in compute.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (compute-efficient allocation predicted from fitted laws; aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: autoregressive pretraining; theoretical prediction from fitted scaling relations
rows.operation_detail: Derived the optimal model-size scaling from L(N,Smin) and the batch-size relation.
rows.measure: Predicted optimal parameter count N(Cmin)
rows.value: N(Cmin) ∝ (Cmin)^0.71
rows.note: The paper says this prediction matches the empirical scaling to within a few percent.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (compute-efficient allocation; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Derived the growth of data processed from the empirical optimal parameter, batch and step trends.
rows.measure: Optimal dataset size D(Cmin)
rows.value: D = B·S; Dopt ∝ Cmin^0.27; De = 2 × 10^10 tokens
rows.note: The paper describes data requirements as growing relatively slowly with compute.

source_check.locator_found: Section 1.2, Equation (1.7); Section 6.1; Table 6, one-epoch Dopt row.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (compute-efficient allocation; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Estimated the number of batch-adjusted training steps at different compute budgets.
rows.measure: Optimal minimum number of training steps Smin(Cmin)
rows.value: Smin ∝ (Cmin)^0.03; Se = 5.4 × 10^3 steps
rows.note: The authors say the small measured exponent may be consistent with zero.

rows.subject: Transformer models (fixed-parameter shape experiments; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Varied selected shape parameters while holding non-embedding parameter count fixed.

conditions.value: depth, width, attention-head dimension, feed-forward ratio

rows.measure: Change in test loss with model shape
rows.baseline: loss for the comparison shape; exact value not stated
rows.value: Loss varies only a few percent over a wide range; Figure 5 describes 22% additional compute as compensating for a 1% loss increase.
rows.note: The text explicitly characterizes shape effects as very mild; exact loss values by configuration are presented graphically.

rows.subject: Transformer models ((nlayer, dmodel) = (6, 4288) and (48, 1600))
rows.operation_detail: Compared two models with different depth-to-width shapes at similar model size.
rows.measure: Test loss difference
rows.value: (6, 4288) reaches a loss within 3% of the (48, 1600) model
rows.note: The paper also says aspect ratio can vary by a factor of 40 while only slightly impacting performance.

rows.subject: Transformer models of varying depth (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared performance trends across depth when embedding parameters were excluded from model size.
rows.measure: Test loss versus non-embedding parameter count
rows.value: Depth variants converge to a single trend, except models with fewer than 2 layers or extreme depth-to-width ratios, which deviate significantly.
rows.note: Shape has little effect in the tested range, with stated exceptions.

rows.subject: Transformer models trained on WebText2 (aggregate evaluation across test distributions)
rows.size_stated: varies; exact sizes not stated for each distribution
rows.stage_stated: pretrained on WebText2; evaluated on other text distributions
rows.operation_detail: Measured held-out cross-entropy against parameter count on text distributions not used for training.
rows.measure: Test loss as a function of non-embedding parameter count
rows.baseline: WebText2 test loss; exact value not stated
rows.value: Loss improves smoothly with model size, with a small, very slowly growing offset from WebText2.
rows.note: The text reports a power law with nearly identical power across the additional text distributions. This is transfer of cross-entropy across text distributions, not downstream task performance.
rows.check: Remove 'none'. Links to V5 only through zero-shot loss on another text distribution. No other modality or fine-tuning is involved.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (joint parameter/dataset fit; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared the fitted exponents from the joint L(N,D) relationship with separate parameter- and dataset-size fits.
rows.measure: Fitted dataset-size exponent αD
rows.value: αD = 0.103 in the joint L(N,D) fit
rows.note: The paper says the difference is slight and results from fitting the full joint relationship rather than the separate limit.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (compute scaling; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared fixed-batch empirical compute scaling with compute scaling adjusted for critical batch size.
rows.measure: Fitted compute-loss exponent
rows.value: αCmin ∼ 0.050 for adjusted Cmin
rows.note: The paper explains that fixed-batch results are not truly optimal and identifies the adjusted measure as more appropriate for prediction.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (small-data joint scaling runs; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated fit quality for L(N,D) on very small dataset subsets.
rows.measure: Fit of the L(N,D) scaling relation
rows.baseline: fit over larger dataset sizes; exact value not stated
rows.value: The fit is poor for the runs with the dataset reduced by a factor of 1024.
rows.note: The authors suggest that this very small dataset may represent a different regime.
rows.check: The state 'absent' is wrong for V7. The poor L(N,D) fit at about 2e7 tokens is a regime where the single law fails, which is in the direction V7 states. It is limited to the tiniest-data runs.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (power-law versus logarithmic fit; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared power-law and logarithmic functional forms for loss versus parameter count.
rows.measure: Qualitative fit accuracy for L(N)
rows.value: Power-law fit is qualitatively much more accurate.
rows.note: The authors also say fit parameters change marginally when some excluded models are included.
rows.check: A comparison of power-law and logarithmic fits bears on the power-law form (V1), not on fit-dependence. The exclusion of 1-layer and unconverged models is said to change fit parameters only marginally.

rows.subject: Transformer language models (compute-efficient scaling extrapolation; aggregate)
rows.size_stated: projected beyond the empirically studied model sizes
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-efficient loss predictions with the data-limited loss implied by the dataset-size law.

conditions.value: projected to scales several orders above those documented

rows.measure: Consistency of L(Cmin) and L(D(Cmin)) predictions
rows.value: The curves are predicted to intersect at C* ∼ 10^4 PF-days, N* ∼ 10^12 parameters, D* ∼ 10^12 tokens, L* ∼ 1.7 nats/token; the authors say the scaling laws must break down at or before this point.
rows.uncertainty: Authors say numerical values are highly uncertain and can vary by an order of magnitude in either direction.
rows.note: This is a derived contradiction and conjecture, not an observed departure in the measured runs.
rows.check: This is a projected contradiction far beyond the measured range. No departure from a power law is observed in the runs; the authors report no deviation at large scale.

tranche.reason: This original study directly measures language-model test cross-entropy across parameter, dataset and compute sweeps and estimates compute-optimal allocation.
